title: Lakeside Cafe Casual
tagline: Small talk that doesn't feel small.
description: Ordering, weather, compliments and the everyday chat of a Lakeside cafe. Keep it light, keep it warm, keep it going.

vibe.scenario: Someone bumps into your table and a drop of your coffee spills.

options.text: Oh, don't worry, that's totally okay — it's only a tiny bit, honestly, it's no problem at all.
Watch where you're going, you ruined my coffee.
Careful — I haven't had my caffeine yet. I bite.

vibe.why: A mock warning turns a tiny accident into a joke you're both in on, and it tells them you're not actually upset.

vibe.scenario: A stranger sheltering next to you from the downpour says, "Great weather, huh?"

options.text: Yeah, it's raining a lot.
It's monsoon. What did you expect?
Pokhara's way of telling us to get another tea.

vibe.why: You played along with their sarcasm and gave the rain a reason. Now you're two people in on the same joke, not two people standing under a roof.

vibe.scenario: A traveller says, "Wow, your English is really good!"

options.text: Thank you.
Why do people always say that? Did you think it would be bad because I'm from Nepal?
Thanks — I practise on tourists. You're doing very well so far.

vibe.why: Accept the compliment, then turn it around with a grin. They stop being the judge and become part of the joke.

vibe.scenario: A nervous new waiter brings you a lemon soda. You ordered masala tea. He looks panicked.

options.text: Honestly, it looks refreshing — but my heart was set on masala tea. No rush.
Sorry, I actually ordered masala tea.
Did you even listen? I said tea.

vibe.why: He's already stressed. A small kindness before the correction, and "no rush" after it, fixes the order without costing him his dignity.

vibe.scenario: A shivering stranger next to you asks, "Worth waking up at four for?"

options.text: Yes, it's nice.
Ask me again after breakfast. Right now the mountains are winning.
Honestly? No. It's freezing, there are two hundred people up here, and the clouds might not even move.

vibe.why: You admit it's early and cold, which makes the compliment to the view feel earned instead of polite.

vibe.scenario: Your friend has just gone to the bathroom. Someone points at their chair: "Is this seat taken?"

options.text: Yes.
It's guarded by my friend's jacket for two more minutes — then it's all yours.
Sorry, my friend is coming back.

vibe.why: Turning the jacket into a tiny security guard makes a "no" feel like a joke, and the promise at the end keeps it friendly.

vibe.scenario: The barista hands you a latte and sighs, "Sorry, it was supposed to be a heart."

options.text: It's abstract. I can feel the love anyway.
Oh, it's completely fine, honestly, it doesn't matter at all — don't worry about it, it tastes the same.
Yeah, it looks nothing like a heart.

vibe.why: You rescued their small failure by calling it art. People remember who made them feel better about a bad moment.

vibe.scenario: A tourist you served last week walks back in: "I'm back! I couldn't find better momos anywhere."

options.text: Thank you, come again.
Other places are terrible anyway.
I know. We ruin people for other momos — it's house policy.

vibe.why: Overclaiming on purpose is funny because it's obviously a bit. Putting down the competition just sounds petty.

vibe.scenario: Mid-conversation with someone new, the power cuts out and the lights die. They laugh nervously.

options.text: Power cut. It happens.
Perfect timing — I was just about to say something clever.
Ugh, this happens all the time here. Honestly, the electricity in this country is a joke.

vibe.why: Making yourself the punchline puts a nervous person at ease. Complaining just drags the mood into the dark with the lights.

vibe.scenario: The traveller at the next table hangs up the phone, eyes wet, and says quietly, "Sorry — bad news from home."

options.text: Cheer up! At least you're in Pokhara.
Oh no, that's a shame.
I'm sorry. Would you like some company, or some quiet?

vibe.why: Charm isn't always a joke. When someone is hurting, the most charming move is to offer a choice and let them lead.

vibe.scenario: A traveller with a laptop asks you, "Is the wifi here any good?"

options.text: Good enough for one photo of the lake. Two if you believe in yourself.
Yes, it works. The password is on the wall behind the counter, next to the menu.
It's Nepal. Don't expect too much.

vibe.why: You answered the real question and turned the slow wifi into a small shared joke instead of an apology.

vibe.scenario: The stranger at the next table gets the exact same order as you: buff momo and hot lemon.

options.text: Great minds. Or we're both very predictable.
Oh, we ordered the same food.
(Look at your phone and say nothing.)

vibe.why: A small coincidence is the easiest opener there is. Name it with a smile and let them decide whether to talk.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "What should I do in Pokhara tomorrow?"

options.text: There are many things: paragliding, boating, Sarangkot, the Peace Pagoda, the caves, Davis Falls, the museums…
Depends. Do you want to fly, float or eat? I can make a strong case for all three.
Just Google it. Everything is online.

vibe.why: A list is information. A question about what they want is a conversation, and it makes your advice fit them.

vibe.scenario: You're having a bad day. The friendly barista asks, "How's your day going?"

options.text: Terrible. Everything is going wrong, my phone broke, my boss is angry, and now it's raining…
Honestly? A bit rough. This coffee is the best part so far — no pressure.
Good, thanks.

vibe.why: You told the truth without dumping it on them, and you gave them a compliment to smile at.

vibe.scenario: Rain starts suddenly. A traveller at the edge of the terrace hasn't noticed their laptop is getting wet.

options.text: Excuse me, it's raining.
Your laptop's about to go swimming — want to grab the table inside with me?
(Watch it get wet. Not your problem.)

vibe.why: Helping someone is the most natural opener in the world. The invite turns a warning into a conversation.

vibe.scenario: A worried traveller asks, "Is it safe to drink the tap water here?"

options.text: Not from the tap, no. Stick to filtered water — lots of cafes will refill your bottle for a few rupees.
Sure, if you want to spend tomorrow in the bathroom! Ha ha, just kidding… actually, I'm not kidding at all.
No.

vibe.why: For health and safety questions, the charming answer is the clear one. Save the jokes for after they have the facts.

vibe.scenario: The waiter tells you the kitchen has run out of the dish you ordered.

options.text: Seriously? It's on the menu. Why is it on the menu if you don't even have it?
Oh, okay. Then I'll just have tea.
No problem. What would you eat if you were me?

vibe.why: Asking for their pick turns a small letdown into a compliment. People love being asked what they know.

vibe.scenario: A tourist keeps dropping momos while trying to eat with a fork and spoon. They look embarrassed.

options.text: Pro tip: nobody here will judge you for using your hands. Half of Pokhara does.
Do you want a different spoon?
Ha, you're really bad at that.

vibe.why: You gave them permission to relax, and a local tip makes them feel like an insider instead of a clumsy tourist.

vibe.scenario: A traveller says, "I love Nepali people. Everyone is so nice!"

options.text: Thank you, that's nice to hear.
Careful, we'll adopt you. People come for one week and somehow stay for a year.
Not everyone. Some people will cheat you, especially the taxi drivers near the lake.

vibe.why: Take the compliment for everyone and give it back as a warm joke. Warnings can wait for when they ask.

vibe.setting: Cafe, end of a long chat
vibe.scenario: You've been talking with a traveller for an hour. You need to leave.

options.text: So… anyway… I should maybe go now… or not… I don't know… okay, bye? Or see you? Bye.
This was the best hour of my week. If you're here tomorrow, the first tea is on me.
Okay, bye! Nice to meet you.

vibe.why: People remember how a conversation ends. A clear, warm exit with a small invitation beats a slow fade.

yesAnd.prompt: You look like you've had a long day.

cards.text: Yeah, I'm tired.
cards.why: Agrees and stops. There's nothing for them to pick up.

cards.text: You have no idea. I'm running on 10% battery and three milk teas.
cards.why: Accepts the premise and adds an image they can play with.

cards.text: Not really.
cards.why: Rejects the premise, so the conversation has to restart from zero.

yesAnd.prompt: This place has the best view in Lakeside.

cards.text: It's okay.
cards.why: Shrugs off their enthusiasm. They'll stop sharing.

cards.text: Agreed. I've been pretending to read this menu for twenty minutes just so I can keep staring.
cards.why: Agrees, then confesses something small and funny. Confessions invite confessions.

yesAnd.prompt: Is it always this hot here?

cards.text: Only until the afternoon rain turns up to apologise.
cards.why: Answers the question and gives the weather a personality.

cards.text: Yes.
cards.why: Technically an answer. Socially, a closed door.

cards.text: Summer is hot and winter is cool, that's how seasons work.
cards.why: Accurate, but it's a weather report. They wanted a chat.

yesAnd.prompt: I think I ate too many momos.

cards.text: You should be careful, they're quite heavy.
cards.why: Sounds like a worried parent. It ends the fun.

cards.text: There's no such thing as too many. There's only "not enough room yet".
cards.why: Rejects the guilt, not the person, and hands them a line to laugh at.

yesAnd.prompt: I'm trying to learn some Nepali.

cards.text: Okay, good.
cards.why: Polite and finished. Nothing to build on.

cards.text: Go on then, say something — I promise to only laugh a little.
cards.why: Invites them to perform, with a tease that makes it feel safe.

cards.text: It's very difficult. Most people give up.
cards.why: Discouraging. You've made them feel silly for trying.

yesAnd.prompt: The traffic on the way here was crazy.

cards.text: Did you get the full experience — the cow in the middle of the road who refuses to move?
cards.why: Adds a shared, specific detail they'll recognise, and asks them to tell the story.

cards.text: Traffic is bad everywhere.
cards.why: Generalises their experience away. Nothing left to say.

cards.text: It's just some random songs.
cards.why: Deflecting the compliment deflates the moment.

cards.text: Stay till three. That's when it quietly turns into 90s Bollywood.
cards.why: Agrees and dangles a reason to stay. That's a hook, not a reply.

cards.text: Welcome.
cards.why: Warm, but it's a full stop.

cards.text: Welcome! So what's the verdict — has Pokhara ruined you for home yet?
cards.why: Welcomes them, then asks a playful question that's easy to answer.

cards.text: Oh, so you haven't seen anything yet.
cards.why: Sounds like you're dismissing their trip before it starts.

cards.text: Thanks! It's survived three treks and one very aggressive monkey.
cards.why: Takes the compliment and hands over a story they'll want to hear.

cards.text: It's really old.
cards.why: Arguing with a compliment makes the giver feel wrong.

yesAnd.prompt: I can't decide what to order.

cards.text: Just pick anything.
cards.why: Unhelpful and a little impatient.

cards.text: Everything is good.
cards.why: Kind, but it doesn't help them decide or give them anything to say back.

cards.text: Tell me your mood and I'll tell you your order. I'm basically a menu fortune-teller.
cards.why: Turns a decision into a little game you play together.

cards.text: Me too.
cards.why: Agrees and stops.

cards.text: Then my work here is done. Dessert arrives in five minutes, whether you like it or not.
cards.why: Plays along and adds a funny threat they can answer.

yesAnd.prompt: This is my last day in Pokhara.

cards.text: Oh, okay. Safe travels.
cards.why: Kind, but it sounds like goodbye already.

cards.text: Then we have to make it count. What's the one thing you haven't done yet?
cards.why: Turns the ending into a small mission you can help with.

cards.text: You should have stayed longer.
cards.why: Too late to be useful, and it sounds like a complaint.

yesAnd.prompt: I can't believe how cheap everything is here.

cards.text: Careful — that's how people end up extending their visa twice. What's the best deal you've found?
cards.why: Light tease, then a question they'll enjoy answering.

cards.text: It's not cheap for us.
cards.why: A fair point, but said like this it lands as a correction and ends the chat.

yesAnd.prompt: I got lost trying to find this place.

cards.text: It's easy, it's just behind the bank.
cards.why: Useful for next time, useless for the conversation.

cards.text: Everyone does. It's our secret test, and you passed. What did you find on the way?
cards.why: Makes getting lost a win and invites their story.

yesAnd.prompt: Is it always this quiet here?

cards.text: Yes.
cards.why: True, maybe. Finished, definitely.

cards.text: Only until the tour buses arrive at noon. Enjoy the peace while it lasts.
cards.why: Adds a little inside knowledge and a picture of what's coming.

yesAnd.prompt: I've been travelling for six months.

cards.text: Six months! Which place still wins, and which one would you never go back to?
cards.why: Two easy, fun questions. Everyone has a favourite and a horror story.

cards.text: Wow, that's long.
cards.why: A reaction, not a reply.

cards.text: Don't you have a job?
cards.why: Sounds like judging, even if you're curious.

yesAnd.pattern: Ask for the best and the worst

upgrader.clunky: I think this place is like, very good, because of the mountains and stuff.
upgrader.why: Lead with what matters, the views. One strong verb and one precise adjective do the work that "like, very good" was reaching for.

upgrader.clunky: Um, so the weather is, like, kind of bad today, maybe we stay inside?
upgrader.why: Name the reason first, then suggest confidently. "Let's" invites. "Maybe we…?" asks permission.

upgrader.clunky: The food was good, I mean, really good, like the best actually.
upgrader.why: Say it once and make it specific. A superlative with a time frame is more believable than three stacked "really"s.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry, sorry, can I maybe get the bill, if it's okay, when you have time?
upgrader.why: One polite frame is enough. Over-apologising makes a normal request sound like a burden.

upgrader.clunky: I don't know, I guess I like Pokhara more than Kathmandu because it's more, like, relaxed?
upgrader.why: Own the opinion, then give it a picture. Ending on an image is stronger than ending on a question mark.

upgrader.clunky: So basically the cafe opens at seven, and basically it closes at like ten.
upgrader.why: Opening hours are information. Give them in one clean sweep. "Basically" added nothing, twice.

upgrader.clunky: It was, um, nice meeting you and stuff, maybe we see each other again sometime?
upgrader.why: Close warmly and definitely. "I hope our paths cross again" leaves the door open without sounding unsure.

upgrader.clunky: The momo here is really, really good, you should like try it.
upgrader.why: Turn the recommendation into a friendly order with a hook. "They're dangerous" makes people curious; "really good" only makes them nod.

upgrader.clunky: I was thinking that, um, maybe we could sit outside because it's sunny?
tiles: grab a table by the water?
answers: grab a table by the water?
upgrader.why: Start with the reason as a bold little claim, then make the offer. "Shall we" is a question that already assumes yes.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry my English is not so good but I will try to explain the menu.
tiles: stop me if anything sounds good.
answers: stop me if anything sounds good.
upgrader.why: Lead with what you'll do, not what you can't. Confidence in the first three words sets the tone for everything after.

upgrader.clunky: Um, do you maybe want to, like, sit here? Only if you want.
upgrader.why: Make the offer, then give a reason. A reason makes it easy to say yes.

upgrader.clunky: The weather is, you know, kind of good today, not too hot, nice.
upgrader.why: Weather talk is boring until you make it specific. Two small pictures make it feel like a real thought.

upgrader.clunky: I'm from here, Pokhara, I was born here, so I know here very well.
upgrader.why: Say it once, then turn it into an offer. "Ask me anything" invites the next question.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry, I think maybe I have seen you before somewhere, maybe?
upgrader.why: A direct question is easier to answer than a nervous one. Two short sentences, no apology.

dropIn.fact: Nepal is home to 8 of the world's 10 highest mountains, including Everest.
dropIn.prompt: A German hiker at the next table groans that the altitude on the Annapurna trail nearly killed them.

options.text: Well, when you've got 8 of the top 10 highest peaks in your backyard, you get used to breathing a little heavier.
options.why: The fact arrives inside a joke about shared suffering. It's about them, not about the fact.

options.text: Did you know Nepal has 8 of the 10 highest mountains in the world?
options.why: True, but it's a quiz question. It moves the conversation away from their story.

options.text: Actually, altitude sickness comes from lower oxygen pressure above about 2,500 metres, so really you should have taken an extra rest day to acclimatise—
options.why: A lecture. They wanted sympathy, not a seminar.

dropIn.fact: Phewa Lake is the second-largest lake in Nepal, after Rara Lake in the far west.
dropIn.prompt: Out on a rowing boat, a tourist spreads their arms: "This lake is huge!"

options.text: Not really, there are much bigger lakes in the world.
options.why: Correcting someone's delight is the fastest way to end it.

options.text: And it's only the runner-up. Rara Lake out west is bigger — Phewa just has better cafes.
options.why: Agrees, adds the fact as a twist, and lands on a local joke.

options.text: It is the second largest lake in Nepal.
options.why: Accurate, but it reads like a signboard.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's flag is the only national flag in the world that isn't a rectangle — it's two stacked pennants.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller points at the flag over the cafe door: "Your flag is so unusual!"

options.text: Yes, it is the only non-rectangular national flag in the world.
options.why: Correct and a bit museum-plaque.

options.text: Everyone else went with rectangles. We took one look at the mountains and went with peaks.
options.why: The fact is implied, not recited, and it comes with a bit of national swagger.

options.text: It's not unusual, it has a very deep meaning. The crimson is for the rhododendron, the blue border is for peace, and the sun and moon represent—
options.why: Contradicting a compliment to deliver a history lesson.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's time zone is UTC+5:45 — fifteen minutes ahead of India, and one of the very few zones offset by 45 minutes.
dropIn.prompt: A just-landed traveller frowns at their phone: "Why does my clock say 11:45? That can't be right."

options.text: Your phone is probably broken.
options.why: Wrong, and it makes them feel silly.

options.text: Nepal's time zone is UTC plus five hours and forty-five minutes.
options.why: Answers the question with the charm of an airport announcement.

options.text: Welcome to Nepal — we run fifteen minutes ahead of India, just to be different.
options.why: Explains the oddity with a wink of national pride.

dropIn.fact: Annapurna I was the first 8,000-metre peak ever climbed, by a French expedition in 1950.
dropIn.prompt: A French couple tells you they can see the Annapurnas from their hotel balcony.

options.text: Then you're in the right place — a French team were the first to climb Annapurna, back in 1950. You're practically visiting family.
options.why: Connects the fact to who they are. People love a story they're part of.

options.text: Annapurna I was first climbed in 1950 by a French expedition led by Maurice Herzog. It was the first 8,000-metre peak anyone ever climbed.
options.why: Right fact, no connection to them.

options.text: Those aren't all Annapurna. The pointy one is Machhapuchhre — tourists always get it wrong.
options.why: Corrects them and lumps them in with "tourists" in one go.

dropIn.fact: Machhapuchhre, the "Fishtail" above Pokhara, is sacred and closed to climbers. A 1957 British team turned back just below the top, and there is no recorded summit.
dropIn.source: Wilfrid Noyce, "Climbing the Fish's Tail" (1958); peak closed to climbing by the Government of Nepal
dropIn.prompt: A climber at the cafe nods at the Fishtail: "Has anyone climbed that one?"

options.text: Why, are you thinking of trying? You'd need a lot more training.
options.why: Teasing their fitness isn't the tease they asked for.

options.text: Nobody's officially stood on top. It's sacred, so it's closed to climbers — the one summit in town that's still just for the gods.
options.why: Gives the fact, the reason, and a line they'll repeat to their friends.

options.text: No, it is closed for climbing because it is a sacred mountain.
options.why: Correct, but flat for such a good story.

dropIn.fact: The rhododendron is Nepal's national flower. In spring, whole hillsides turn red and pink.
dropIn.source: Government of Nepal, national symbols; Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Nepal"
dropIn.prompt: A trekker shows you a photo from the trail: "What are these amazing red trees?"

options.text: Just rhododendrons. They're everywhere here.
options.why: "Just" shrinks their wonder. Let them be amazed.

options.text: Rhododendrons — the national flower. Come April, the whole hillside basically shows off.
options.why: Names it, gives it status, and makes the mountain sound like it has a personality.

options.text: That is the rhododendron, which is the national flower of Nepal. It grows at many different altitudes and blooms mainly in spring.
options.why: Right answer, textbook delivery.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's official calendar, Bikram Sambat, runs about 56 years and 8 months ahead of the Gregorian calendar. The Nepali new year falls in mid-April.
dropIn.source: Government of Nepal official calendar (Bikram Sambat); Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Vikrama era"
dropIn.prompt: A confused traveller holds up the local newspaper: "Why does this say 2083?"

options.text: Relax, you haven't time-travelled. Well — a little. Our calendar runs about 57 years ahead, so technically you're in the future.
options.why: Turns confusion into a small thrill. They'll tell this one at home.

options.text: Nepal uses the Bikram Sambat calendar, which is about 57 years ahead.
options.why: Explains it, doesn't enjoy it.

options.text: Everyone knows Nepal has a different calendar.
options.why: Clearly not everyone. Now they feel foolish.

dropIn.fact: Nepal grows tea in Ilam, in the far east, on the same hills that continue into Darjeeling across the border in India.
dropIn.source: National Tea and Coffee Development Board, Nepal
dropIn.prompt: A British tea lover takes a sip: "This is lovely. Is it Darjeeling?"

options.text: Close — it's from Ilam, just over the border. Same hills, same mist, less famous.
options.why: Accepts their good guess, corrects gently, and gives Nepali tea an underdog charm.

options.text: No, it's Nepali tea from Ilam, near Darjeeling.
options.why: Fine, but it starts with "no".

options.text: No, no — Darjeeling is in India. This is Nepali tea. People always assume good tea must be Darjeeling, but Nepal grows its own.
options.why: A good guess met with a flat correction and a border dispute.

dropIn.fact: The Buddha was born in Lumbini, in southern Nepal. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
dropIn.source: UNESCO World Heritage List, "Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha"
dropIn.prompt: A traveller in a Buddha T-shirt says, "I always thought the Buddha was Indian."

options.text: No! He was Nepali. People get this wrong all the time and it's very annoying.
options.why: Right fact, wrong temperature. They'll remember the scolding, not Lumbini.

options.text: Easy mistake — he was born in Lumbini, a few hours south of here, and then went travelling. Like you.
options.why: Corrects without heat and ends on a connection to them.

options.text: Actually, the Buddha was born in Lumbini, in Nepal.
options.why: Correct. The "actually" does a little damage.

wordPower.sentence: The view from this cafe is very nice.

options.text: stunning
options.why: Strong, clear, and every traveller knows it.

options.text: resplendent
options.why: Correct, but many travellers won't know this word.

options.text: good
options.why: Even flatter than "very nice".

wordPower.example: The sunrise from Sarangkot was stunning.

wordPower.sentence: This lemon tea is really good.

options.text: okay
options.why: Sounds like a complaint.

options.text: delectable
options.why: Right meaning, but it sounds like a food critic.

options.text: perfect
options.why: Short, warm and easy to understand anywhere.

wordPower.example: The weather is perfect for the boat today.

wordPower.sentence: I am very tired after the trek.

options.text: exhausted
options.why: One word that says "very, very tired".

options.text: enervated
options.why: Correct, but rare. People will look confused.

options.text: a bit sleepy
options.why: Much weaker than what you mean.

wordPower.meaning: Extremely tired, with no energy left.
wordPower.example: After eight hours of walking, everyone was exhausted.

wordPower.sentence: Lakeside was very busy last night.

options.text: normal
options.why: The opposite of what you mean.

options.text: packed
options.why: Vivid and simple. You can almost see the crowd.

options.text: thronged
options.why: Correct, but old-fashioned for a chat.

wordPower.meaning: So full of people there's hardly any space.
wordPower.example: The bus to Kathmandu was packed.

wordPower.sentence: Your story about the monkey was really funny.

options.text: hilarious
options.why: Says "I really laughed" in one word.

options.text: risible
options.why: Rare, and it usually means "silly in a bad way".

options.text: amusing
options.why: Polite, but it sounds like you only smiled a little.

wordPower.meaning: So funny it makes you laugh out loud.
wordPower.example: The guide's stories on the bus were hilarious.

options.text: sweltering
options.why: A good word, but less common than the best one.

options.text: warm
options.why: Too weak. Warm is nice; you mean too much.

options.text: boiling
options.why: Everyday, funny and very clear.

wordPower.example: It's boiling in the bus park at noon.

wordPower.sentence: The bus ride from Kathmandu was very bad.

options.text: a nightmare
options.why: Everyone understands it, and it tells a story.

options.text: unpleasant
options.why: Correct, but polite and flat.

options.text: execrable
options.why: Too rare. Most people won't know it.

wordPower.example: Finding a taxi in the rain was a nightmare.

wordPower.sentence: My landlady is a very nice person.

options.text: amiable
options.why: Right meaning, but a bit formal.

options.text: okay
options.why: Sounds like you don't really like her.

options.text: lovely
options.why: Warm and very natural in spoken English.

wordPower.example: The family at the homestay were lovely.

wordPower.sentence: The lake is very quiet in the morning.

options.text: perfectly still
options.why: Paints a picture: no wind, no waves, a mirror.

options.text: tranquil
options.why: Nice word, but a little like a hotel brochure.

options.text: empty
options.why: A different meaning, and a bit sad.

wordPower.meaning: Not moving at all. Calm like a mirror.
wordPower.example: At six in the morning, Phewa is perfectly still.

wordPower.sentence: I really like this little cafe.

options.text: don't mind
options.why: Means you're only okay with it.

options.text: love
options.why: Short, warm and completely natural.

options.text: am enamoured of
options.why: Correct, but it sounds like poetry.

wordPower.example: I love how quiet it is here after the rain.
